title: Recording: Give Ireland Back To The Irish by Wings | 1972
content:
Studio Three, EMI Studios, Abbey Road
Producer: Paul McCartney
Engineer: Tony Clark

Wings began recording their debut single, ‘Give Ireland Back To The Irish’, on 1 February 1972.

Paul McCartney had written the song the day before, in response to Bloody Sunday, also known as the Bogside Massacre, in which British soldiered opened fire on unarmed civilians during a protest march in Derry, Northern Ireland. It was the worst mass shooting in Northern Irish history, and worsened the conflict between Irish nationalists and the British Army.

McCartney wished to record the song quickly, and decided that Wings would turn up at EMI Studios at Abbey Road and find an empty studio without booking. Wings had rehearsed earlier in the day, at McCartney’s Cavendish Avenue home and again at the Institute of Contemporary Arts.

Wings found Studio Three at Abbey Road empty upon their 6pm arrival. Technical assistant Mark Vigars was still in the building, and he called Tony Clark to engineer the session.

It was a very late booking. In fact, it wasn’t booked. My parents had a bungalow down at Cliftonville in Kent, and I’d been there with my two daughters. My dad was teaching me to drive. We drove back, feeling very pleased, thinking I’ll be all right, I’ll pass my test here. Then, my wife’s outside our house, waving, and she says, ‘Mark Vigars has just phoned up and you’ve got to go into the studio.’ I thought, ‘But it’s Tuesday afternoon – what do you mean, they want me in the studio?’ I just didn’t know what to do.

Then I thought, ‘Oh, sod it, I think it’ll be worse, the repercussions of not doing it.’ So, I decided to go. I came by train and the tube, and as I was walking down from St John’s Wood tube station towards the zebra crossing I could hear it coming out of the building. I thought – it’s got to be loud in there – you could hear it outside. It was really loud.

Tony Clark, 16 February 2017
The McCartney Legacy: Volume 1: 1969-73, Allan Kozinn, Adrian Sinclair

The session was documented by music journalist Andrew Tyler, of Disc and Music Echo. Tyler captured the ramshackle background to the recording:

Many hours later there was the debris of stoned, sleep-hungry bodies strewn over chairs in the sound room. Linda was asleep across her husband’s back; Henry and the Dennys could have used matchsticks to prop open their eyes and Paul McCartney was tapping out rhythms and playing with dials on the space-age control panel…

10p.m. Tony’s ready at last. They try a take but listening in on the replay sense they’ve lost something.

‘We should’ve done it this afternoon when it was still fresh,’ says Denny L. Paul agrees: ‘We’ve lost some of the feel but it’s a better sound.’ He calls through the monitor to Tony: ‘Couldn’t you make it sound like a record. Something more electric. It sounds too much like a band.’

As the night wears thin he wages a subtle battle to arrest control of the sound panel from Tony. Eventually he dominates as he dominates every other situation. By this time Henry has come through with a superb guitar line for the intro and verse. Denny supports with a compact rhythm that serves as a second lead and Linda backs with choppy chording on piano.

Andrew Tyler
Disc and Music Echo, 12 February 1972

The recording session ended at around 5.30am. Although a backing track had been completed, more overdubs were recorded on 3 February.
